::: {#exm-skeptical-prior}
#### A skeptical prior for a Gaussian mean

In the model of @exm-normal-normal,
replace the $\ndist{0, 1}$ prior by the [skeptical prior](#def-skeptical-prior)
$\mean \sim \ndist{0, \sdprior^2}$,
whose standard deviation $\sdprior$ sets how skeptical it is.
Its density is proportional to $\expf{-\frac{1}{2}\mean^2/\sdprior^2}$.
Let $m_\sdprior \eqdef \frac{n \bar x}{n + 1/\sdprior^2}$.
Reusing the likelihood from @exm-normal-normal:

$$
\ba
\p(\mean \mid \vx)
&\propto \expf{-\frac{1}{2}\paren{n \mean^2 - 2 \mean n \bar x}}
  \cdot \expf{-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\mean^2}{\sdprior^2}}
&& \text{(likelihood times prior)}\\
&= \expf{-\frac{1}{2}\paren{\paren{n + \frac{1}{\sdprior^2}}\mean^2 - 2 \mean n \bar x}}
&& \text{(adding exponents)}\\
&= \expf{-\frac{1}{2}\paren{n + \frac{1}{\sdprior^2}}\paren{\mean^2 - 2 \mean m_\sdprior}}
&& \text{(factoring; definition of $m_\sdprior$)}\\
&= \expf{-\frac{1}{2}\paren{n + \frac{1}{\sdprior^2}}\paren{(\mean - m_\sdprior)^2 - m_\sdprior^2}}
&& \text{(completing the square)}\\
&\propto \expf{-\frac{1}{2}\paren{n + \frac{1}{\sdprior^2}}(\mean - m_\sdprior)^2}
&& \text{(dropping a factor that does not involve $\mean$)}.
\ea
$$

So $\mean \mid \vx \sim \ndist{m_\sdprior,\; 1 / (n + 1/\sdprior^2)}$,
and $\sdprior = 1$ recovers @exm-normal-normal.
The posterior mean

$$
m_\sdprior = \frac{n \cdot \bar x + \frac{1}{\sdprior^2} \cdot 0}{n + \frac{1}{\sdprior^2}}
$$

is a weighted average of the sample mean and the prior mean $0$,
weighted by the precision $n$ of the data and the precision $1/\sdprior^2$ of the prior
(a precision is a reciprocal variance).
The more skeptical the prior (the smaller $\sdprior$),
the more the posterior mean shrinks toward $0$.
With $\bar x = 2$ and $n = 20$ held fixed:

```{r}
#| label: skeptical-prior
#| code-fold: false
xbar <- 2
n <- 20
tau <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 10)
data.frame(prior_sd = tau, posterior_mean = n * xbar / (n + 1 / tau^2)) |>
  round(3)
```

The most skeptical prior ($\sdprior = 0.1$) pulls the posterior mean
down to one sixth of the sample mean,
while the most diffuse ($\sdprior = 10$) leaves it essentially at $\bar x$.
:::
